prompt:
A colleague reasons: "Every request yesterday was served from the cache or from the database. Therefore either every request was served from the cache, or every request was served from the database." Is this valid?

*Symbols: ∨ means OR (inclusive); ∀ means "for all".*

options.explanation: ∀ distributes over ∧, not ∨. for every x (P or Q) can hold with some x satisfying only P and others only Q.

options.text: No: for every x (P or Q) does not imply for every x P or for every x Q
options.explanation: Correct. A day with some cached requests and some misses makes the premise true and both disjuncts of the conclusion false.

options.text: Yes, provided there was at least one request
options.explanation: A non-empty domain doesn't help: two requests, one hit and one miss, already break it.

options.text: No, because the premise uses inclusive or
options.explanation: Inclusive or is not the problem; the same counterexample works with exclusive or. The error is distributing ∀ over ∨.

workedExample: Use two requests: one served only by cache and one only by the database. Each has a permitted source, so the premise holds. Neither source served every request, so the conclusion fails.

prompt:
Which of these implications are valid in **every** non-empty domain, for every choice of P and Q? Select all that apply.

*Symbols: ∧ means AND; → means "implies" (if ... then); ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: there exists y for every x P(x, y) implies for every x there exists y P(x, y)
options.explanation: Correct. If one y works for every x, then for each x that same y is a witness.

options.text: for every x there exists y P(x, y) implies there exists y for every x P(x, y)
options.explanation: Invalid. Over the integers with P(x, y) equals y is greater than x, the left side is true and the right side would need a largest integer.

options.text: there exists x (P(x) and Q(x)) implies there exists x P(x) and there exists x Q(x)
options.explanation: Correct. The single witness for P and Q serves as a witness for P and for Q.

options.text: there exists x P(x) and there exists x Q(x) implies there exists x (P(x) and Q(x))
options.explanation: Invalid. There is an even integer and an odd integer, but no integer is both. The two witnesses can differ.

options.text: for every x (P(x) and Q(x)) implies for every x P(x)
options.explanation: Correct. ∀ distributes over ∧, so for every x (P and Q) gives for every x P (and for every x Q).

workedExample: A common witness can be reused for each input, but separate witnesses cannot generally be merged. One object satisfying both properties proves each exists; separate even and odd integers do not give an integer that is both. Finally, every object having both properties necessarily means every object has the first.
